eras.name: Creation
eras.eraDescription: The primordial age when the cosmos was formed from chaos. Tiamat and Apsu existed before all others.

eras.name: Age of the First Gods
eras.eraDescription: The great gods emerged — Anu took the heavens, Enlil the earth, Enki the waters.

eras.name: Anunnaki on Earth
eras.eraDescription: The Anunnaki descended to Earth, established cities, and began mining operations according to Sumerian texts.

eras.name: Creation of Mankind
eras.eraDescription: Humans were created to relieve the gods of labor. Enki and Ninhursag fashioned mankind from clay.

eras.name: Antediluvian Period
eras.eraDescription: The age of the antediluvian kings with impossibly long reigns, as recorded in the Sumerian King List.

eras.name: The Great Flood
eras.eraDescription: Enlil sent the deluge to destroy mankind. Ziusudra survived by building an ark on Enki's warning.

eras.name: Post-Flood Kingdoms
eras.eraDescription: Kingship descended from heaven again. The dynasties of Kish, Uruk, and Ur arose.

eras.name: Early Dynastic Period
eras.eraDescription: Historical kings emerge alongside legendary ones. Gilgamesh rules Uruk. The gods still intervene directly.

eras.name: SKL Antediluvian
eras.eraDescription: The mythical kings who ruled before the Great Flood, with reigns lasting tens of thousands of years.

eras.name: First dynasty of Kish
eras.eraDescription: The first dynasty to receive kingship after the Flood according to the Sumerian King List.

eras.name: First rulers of Uruk
eras.eraDescription: The early rulers of Uruk, including the legendary Mesh-ki-ang-gasher, Enmerkar, and Lugalbanda.

eras.name: First dynasty of Ur
eras.eraDescription: The first dynasty of the city of Ur, including Mesh-Ane-pada.

eras.name: Dynasty of Awan
eras.eraDescription: An Elamite dynasty from the region of Awan that briefly held kingship.

eras.name: Second dynasty of Kish
eras.eraDescription: The second dynasty of Kish, including rulers with epithets like 'the fuller' and 'the boatman'.

eras.name: Dynasty of Hamazi
eras.eraDescription: A dynasty from the city of Hamazi in the Zagros region.

eras.name: Second dynasty of Uruk
eras.eraDescription: The second dynasty of Uruk, including En-shag-kush-ana.

eras.name: Second dynasty of Ur
eras.eraDescription: The second dynasty of Ur, including Nanni and his son Mesh-ki-ang-Nanna.

eras.name: Dynasty of Adab
eras.eraDescription: The dynasty of the city of Adab, including Lugal-Ane-mundu.

eras.name: Dynasty of Mari
eras.eraDescription: The dynasty of the city of Mari, including Anbu, Anba, Bazi, and others.

eras.name: Third dynasty of Kish
eras.eraDescription: The third dynasty of Kish, including the only woman on the King List: Kug-Bau.

eras.name: Dynasty of Akshak
eras.eraDescription: The dynasty of the city of Akshak, including Puzur-Nirah and Shu-Suen (Akshak).

eras.name: Fourth dynasty of Kish
eras.eraDescription: The fourth dynasty of Kish, including Puzur-Suen (Kish) and Ur-Zababa. Sargon was Ur-Zababa's cup-bearer.

eras.name: Third dynasty of Uruk
eras.eraDescription: The third dynasty of Uruk, including Lugal-zage-si who ruled all of Sumer.

eras.name: Dynasty of Akkad
eras.eraDescription: The Akkadian Empire founded by Sargon, the first empire in history.

eras.name: Fourth dynasty of Uruk
eras.eraDescription: The fourth dynasty of Uruk, including Ur-nigin, Ur-gigir, and Ur-Utu.

eras.name: Gutian rule
eras.eraDescription: The rule of Gutian kings from the Zagros mountains over Mesopotamia.

eras.name: Fifth dynasty of Uruk
eras.eraDescription: The fifth dynasty of Uruk, including Utu-hengal who drove out the Gutians.

eras.name: Third dynasty of Ur
eras.eraDescription: The Neo-Sumerian Ur III empire, including Ur-Namma, Shulgi, and Shu-Suen.

eras.name: Dynasty of Isin
eras.eraDescription: The Isin dynasty that ruled after the fall of Ur, including Ishbi-Erra and Lipit-Eshtar.

eras.name: Age of the Watchers
eras.eraDescription: The antediluvian age when 200 Watcher angels descended on Mount Hermon, took human wives, fathered the Nephilim, and taught humanity forbidden knowledge. Ended with the Great Flood as divine judgment.

figures.name: Tiamat
figures.title: Primordial Mother of the Gods
figures.figureDescription: The primordial goddess of the salt sea. Her body was split by Marduk to form heaven and earth.

figures.name: Apsu
figures.title: Primordial Father
figures.figureDescription: The primordial god of fresh water beneath the earth. Slain by Enki/Ea who built his temple upon him.

figures.name: Anshar
figures.title: Whole Sky
figures.figureDescription: Primordial god representing the whole sky. Father of Anu.

figures.name: Kishar
figures.title: Whole Earth
figures.figureDescription: Primordial goddess representing the whole earth. Mother of Anu.

figures.name: Anu
figures.title: King of the Gods, Father of the Heavens
figures.figureDescription: Supreme god of the Sumerian/Akkadian pantheon. Ruled from the heavens. Father of Enlil, Enki, and many others.

figures.name: Antu
figures.title: Queen of the Heavens
figures.figureDescription: Consort of Anu and mother goddess of the heavens.

figures.name: Enlil
figures.title: Lord of the Wind, King of the Earth
figures.figureDescription: Chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon after Anu. Commander of the Anunnaki on Earth. Decreed the Flood.

figures.name: Ninlil
figures.title: Lady of the Wind
figures.figureDescription: Consort of Enlil. Mother of Nanna the moon god.

figures.name: Enki
figures.title: Lord of the Earth, God of Wisdom
figures.figureDescription: God of wisdom, fresh water, and creation. Warned Ziusudra of the Flood. Co-created humans with Ninhursag.

figures.name: Ninhursag
figures.title: Lady of the Mountain
figures.figureDescription: Mother goddess. Worked with Enki to create mankind from clay mixed with divine blood.

figures.name: Nanna
figures.title: Lord of the Moon
figures.figureDescription: Moon god, son of Enlil and Ninlil. Father of Utu and Inanna. Chief deity of Ur.

figures.name: Ningal
figures.title: Great Lady
figures.figureDescription: Consort of Nanna. Mother of Utu and Inanna.

figures.name: Utu
figures.title: Sun God, Lord of Justice
figures.figureDescription: Sun god and divine judge. Aided Gilgamesh in his quest against Humbaba.

figures.name: Inanna
figures.title: Queen of Heaven
figures.figureDescription: Goddess of love, beauty, sex, war, and political power. Descended to the underworld and returned.

figures.name: Marduk
figures.title: King of the Gods (Babylon)
figures.figureDescription: Chief deity of Babylon. Slew Tiamat and created the world from her body. Son of Enki/Ea.

figures.name: Nabu
figures.title: God of Scribes
figures.figureDescription: God of writing and wisdom. Son of Marduk. Patron of scribes and scholars.

figures.name: Ereshkigal
figures.title: Queen of the Underworld
figures.figureDescription: Ruler of the underworld (Kur/Irkalla). Sister of Inanna. Held power over the dead.

figures.name: Nergal
figures.title: Lord of the Underworld
figures.figureDescription: God of war and plague who became co-ruler of the underworld with Ereshkigal.

figures.name: Ninurta
figures.title: Lord of the Plow
figures.figureDescription: Warrior god and god of agriculture. Son of Enlil. Defeated the Anzu bird.

figures.name: Dumuzi
figures.title: The Shepherd King
figures.figureDescription: Shepherd god and consort of Inanna. Sent to the underworld as her substitute.

figures.name: Adapa
figures.title: First Sage
figures.figureDescription: First of the Seven Sages (Apkallu). Created by Enki as a model human. Refused the food of immortality.

figures.name: Ziusudra
figures.title: He Who Found Long Life
figures.figureDescription: Survivor of the Great Flood. Warned by Enki, he built an ark. Granted immortality by the gods afterward.

figures.name: Gilgamesh
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Two-thirds divine, one-third human. King of Uruk who sought eternal life after the death of Enkidu. According to the Sumerian King List, ruled for 126 years.
figures.source: Epic of Gilgamesh, Sumerian King List

figures.name: Lugalbanda
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Legendary king of Uruk. Father of Gilgamesh. Deified after death. According to the Sumerian King List, ruled for 1,200 years (mythological length).

figures.name: Ninsun
figures.title: Lady Wild Cow
figures.figureDescription: Goddess and mother of Gilgamesh. Known for her wisdom and ability to interpret dreams.

figures.name: Enkidu
figures.title: Wild Man, Friend of Gilgamesh
figures.figureDescription: Created by the gods from clay as a companion and equal to Gilgamesh. Raised among animals.

figures.name: Sarpanit
figures.title: Lady of Babylon, Shining One
figures.figureDescription: Consort of Marduk and chief goddess of Babylon. Mother of Nabu. Central figure in the Akitu New Year festival. Worshipped in the Esagila temple.

figures.name: Alulim
figures.title: King of Sumerian King List
figures.figureDescription: Alulim (Sumerian: 𒀉𒇻𒅆, romanized: Álulim; transliterated: a₂.lu.lim) was a mythological Mesopotamian ruler, regarded as the first king ever to rule. He is known from the Sumerian King List, Ballad of Early Rulers, and other similar sources which invariably place him in Eridu and assign a reign to him lasting tens of thousands of years. The tablet of Old Babylonian period (c. (Listed reign: 28,800 years.)

figures.name: Alalngar
figures.title: King of Sumerian King List
figures.figureDescription: Alalngar was the second king to exercise the kingship of Eridu over all of Sumer—according to the Sumerian King List (SKL). He may have ruled c. 2866 – c. (Listed reign: 36,000 years.)

figures.name: En-men-lu-ana
figures.title: King of Sumerian King List
figures.figureDescription: En-men-lu-ana appears as the first king of Bad-tibira in a version of the Sumerian King List. The list claims that En-men-lu-ana ruled for c. 43,200 years, and was succeeded by En-men-gal-ana. (Listed reign: 43,200 years.)

figures.name: En-men-gal-ana
figures.title: King of Sumerian King List
figures.figureDescription: En-men-gal-ana appears as the second king of Bad-tibira in some versions of the Sumerian King List. According to that literary composition, En-men-gal-ana ruled for 28,800 years. The kings on the early part of the SKL are usually not considered historical, except when they are mentioned in Early Dynastic documents. (Listed reign: 28,800 years.)

figures.name: Dumuzid
figures.title: King of Sumerian King List
figures.figureDescription: Dumuzid, Dumuzi, or Tammuz (Sumerian: 𒌉𒍣, romanized: Dumuzid; Akkadian: Duʾūzu, Dûzu; Arabic: تمّوز, romanized: Tammuz, Tammūz; Hebrew: תַּמּוּז, romanized: Tammūz; Syriac: ܬܵܡܘܿܙ, romanized: Tāmōz), known to the Sumerians as Dumuzid the Shepherd (Sumerian: 𒌉𒍣𒉺𒇻, romanized: Dumuzid sipad) and to the Canaanites as Adon (Phoenician: 𐤀𐤃𐤍; Proto-Hebrew: 𐤀𐤃𐤍), is an ancient Mesopotamian and Levantine deity associated with agriculture and shepherds, who was also the first and primary consort of the goddess Inanna (later known as Ishtar). In Sumerian mythology, Dumuzid's sister was Geshtinanna, the goddess of agriculture, fertility, and dream interpretation. In the Sumerian King List, Dumuzid is listed as an antediluvian king of the city of Bad-tibira and also an early king of the city of Uruk. (Listed reign: 36,000 years.)

figures.name: En-sipad-zid-ana
figures.title: King of Sumerian King List
figures.figureDescription: En-sipad-zid-ana appears as the king of Larak in some versions of the Sumerian King List (SKL). According to that literary composition, En-sipad-zid-ana ruled for 28,800 years. The kings on the early part of the SKL are usually not considered historical, except when they are mentioned in Early Dynastic documents. (Listed reign: 28,800 years.)

figures.name: En-men-dur-ana
figures.title: King of Sumerian King List
figures.figureDescription: En-men-dur-ana (also En-men-dur-an-ki, Enmenduranki) of Zimbir (the city now known as Sippar) was an ancient Sumerian king, whose name appears in the Sumerian King List as the seventh pre-dynastic king of Sumer. He was also the topic of myth and legend, said to have reigned for around 21,000 years. (Listed reign: 21,000 years.)

figures.name: Ubara-Tutu
figures.title: King of Sumerian King List
figures.figureDescription: Ubara-tutu (or Ubartutu) of Shuruppak was the last antediluvian king of Sumer, according to some versions of the Sumerian King List. He was said to have reigned for 18,600 years (5 sars and 1 ner). He was the son of En-men-dur-ana, a Sumerian mythological figure often compared to Enoch, as he entered heaven without dying. (Listed reign: 18,600 years.)

figures.name: Jushur
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Jushur (cuneiform: 𒄑𒃡 ĜIŠ.UR3; Sumerian: Ĝušur) appears as a king of Kish in the Sumerian king list, a literary composition created in Mesopotamia at the beginning of the second millennium BC. He is either the first king on the list to be mentioned, or the first king after a flood, depending on the version of the SKL. According to the list, Jushur reigned for 1,200 years. (Listed reign: 1,200 years.)

figures.name: Kullassina-bel
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Kullassina-bel of Kish was the second king in the First Dynasty of Kish according to the Sumerian king list, which adds that he reigned for 960 years (or 900 in some copies). (Listed reign: 960 years.)

figures.name: Nangishlishma
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Nangishlishma of Kish (also written as  Nanjiclicma) was the third Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish,who reigned for around 670 years according to some versions of the Sumerian king list. His name does not appear in Early Dynastic inscriptions, meaning that he is unlikely to have been a real historical person. (Listed reign: 670 years.)

figures.name: En-tarah-ana
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: En-tarah-ana of Kish was the fourth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. The Weld-Blundell Prism was damaged at this point, so Thorkild Jacobsen had restored this ruler's name as Bahina. En-tarah-ana is unlikely to have existed as his name does not appear on texts dating from the period in which he was presumed to have lived (Early Dynastic period). (Listed reign: 420 years.)

figures.name: Babum
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Babum of Kish was the fifth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. Babum is unlikely to have existed as his name does not appear on texts dating from the period in which he was presumed to have lived (Early Dynastic period). Like other leader of the first dynasty, his name is an Akkadian word, bābum meaning "gate". (Listed reign: 300 years.)

figures.name: Puannum
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the First dynasty of Kish. Reigned 840 years (mythological length). (Listed reign: 840 years.)

figures.name: Kalibum
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Kalibum of Kish was the seventh Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. This name is written "Ga-lí-bu-um ... normalized as Kalibum", and is believed to be derived from the Akkadian for 'hound'. (Listed reign: 960 years.)

figures.name: Kalumum
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Kalumum (Sumerian:𒅗𒇻𒈬𒌝) of Kish was the eighth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. Like the other members of the First dynasty prior to Etana, he was named for an animal; his name "Kalumun" is Akkadian for "lamb". Kalulum is unlikely to have existed as his name does not appear on texts dating from the period in which he was presumed to have lived (Early Dynastic period). (Listed reign: 840 years.)

figures.name: Zuqaqip
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the First dynasty of Kish. Reigned 900 years (mythological length). (Listed reign: 900 years.)

figures.name: Atab
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Atab of Kish was the tenth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. His successor was his son Mashda. Atab is unlikely to have existed as his name does not appear on texts dating from the period in which he was presumed to have lived (Early Dynastic period). (Listed reign: 600 years.)

figures.name: Mashda
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Mashda of Kish was the eleventh Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. He was a son of the king Atab. Like the other members of the First dynasty prior to Etana, he was named for an animal; his name "Mashda" is Akkadian for "gazelle". (Listed reign: 840 years.)

figures.name: Arwium
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Arwium of Kish was the twelfth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. His father was Mashda, the previous ruler. Like the other members of the First dynasty prior to Etana, he was named for an animal; his name "Arwium" is Akkadian for "male gazelle". (Listed reign: 720 years.)

figures.name: Etana
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Etana (𒂊𒋫𒈾, E.TA.NA) was the thirteenth king of the first dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian King List. He is listed as the successor of Arwium, the son of Mashda, as king of Kish. The list also calls Etana "the shepherd, who ascended to heaven and consolidated all the foreign countries", and states that he ruled 1,500 years (some copies read 635) before being succeeded by his son Balih, said to have ruled 400 years.

figures.name: Balih
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Balih of Kish was the fourteenth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. His father was Etana, whom he succeeded as ruler. The kings on the early part of the SKL are usually not considered historical, except when they are mentioned in Early Dynastic documents. (Listed reign: 400 years.)

figures.name: En-me-nuna
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: En-me-nuna of Kish was the fifteenth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian King List. The kings on the early part of the SKL are usually not considered historical, except when they are mentioned in Early Dynastic documents. En-me-nuna is not one of them. (Listed reign: 660 years.)

figures.name: Melem-Kish
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Melem-Kish of Kish was the sixteenth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian King List (SKL). His father was En-me-nuna, whom he succeeded as ruler. The kings on the early part of the SKL are usually not considered historical, except when they are mentioned in Early Dynastic documents. (Listed reign: 900 years.)

figures.name: Barsal-nuna
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Barsal-nuna (Sumerian: 𒁇𒊩𒉣𒈾 bar.sal.nun.na) of Kish was the seventeenth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian King List. His father was En-me-nuna; he succeeded his brother Melem-Kish. His name may have meant Sheep of the Prince. (Listed reign: 1,200 years.)

figures.name: Zamug
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Zamug of Kish was the eighteenth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian king list. His father was Barsal-nuna, whom he succeeded as ruler. His name does not appear in documents other than the SKL, meaning that it is unlikely that he was a historical person.

figures.name: Tizqar
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Tizqar of Kish was the nineteenth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish and succeeded his father Zamuq as ruler, according to some versions of the Sumerian King List. His name does not appear in Early Dynastic inscriptions, meaning that he is unlikely to have been a real historical person. (Listed reign: 305 years.)

figures.name: Ilku
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ilku of Kish was the twentieth Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian King List. His name does not appear in Early Dynastic inscriptions, meaning that he is unlikely to have been a real historical person. (Listed reign: 900 years.)

figures.name: Iltasadum
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Iltasadum of Kish was the 21st Sumerian king in the First Dynasty of Kish, according to the Sumerian King List. His name does not appear in Early Dynastic inscriptions, meaning that he is unlikely to have been a real historical person. (Listed reign: 1,200 years.)

figures.name: Enmebaragesi
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Enmebaragesi (Sumerian: 𒂗𒈨𒁈𒄄𒋛 Enmebárgisi [EN-ME-BARA2-GI4-SE]; fl. c. 2750 BC) originally Mebarasi (𒈨𒁈𒋛) was the penultimate king of the first dynasty of Kish and is recorded as having reigned 900 years in the Sumerian King List. (Listed reign: 900 years.)

figures.name: Aga of Kish
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Aga (Sumerian: 𒀝𒂵 Aga, Agga, or Akkà; fl. c. 2700 BC), commonly known as Aga of Kish, was king in the first dynasty of Kish during the Early Dynastic I period. (Listed reign: 625 years.)

figures.name: Mesh-ki-ang-gasher
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the First rulers of Uruk. Reigned 324 years (mythological length). Late Uruk Period (Listed reign: 324 years.)

figures.name: Enmerkar
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Enmerkar (fl. c. 2750 BC) was an ancient Sumerian ruler to whom the construction of the city of Uruk and a 420-year reign was attributed. (Listed reign: 420 years.)

figures.name: Dumuzid the Fisherman
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Dumuzid, titled the Fisherman, was a legendary Sumerian king of Uruk listed originating from Kuara. According to legend, in the 100th year of his reign, he was captured by Enmebaragesi.

figures.name: Ur-Nungal
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Ur-Nungal (died c. 2620 BC) was the sixth Sumerian ruler in the First Dynasty of Uruk, according to the Sumerian King List, which also claims he ruled 30 years. Both the Sumerian King List and the Tummal Chronicle state he was the son of Gilgamesh, but only the Sumerian King List records he was the father of Udul-kalama.

figures.name: Udul-kalama
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Udul-kalama (died c. 2605 BC) was the seventh Sumerian ruler in the First Dynasty of Uruk, according to the Sumerian King List. He may have been a son of Ur-Nungal and grandson of Gilgamesh.

figures.name: La-ba'shum
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: La-ba'shum (died c. 2596 BC) was the eighth Sumerian ruler in the First Dynasty of Uruk, according to the Sumerian King List. He was described as ruling for nine years.

figures.name: En-nun-tarah-ana
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: En-nun-tarah-ana (died c. 2588 BC) was the ninth Sumerian ruler in the First Dynasty of Uruk. According to the Sumerian King List, he reigned for 8 years.

figures.name: Mesh-he
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Mesh-He (died c. 2552 BC), described as "the smith", is the 10th lugal of the first dynasty of Uruk. He ruled in modern-day Iraq.

figures.name: Melem-ana
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Melem-Ana of Unug (died c. 2546 BC) was the 11th lugal of the First Dynasty of Uruk. He ruled in Mesopotamia in what is now Iraq.

figures.name: Lugal-kitun
figures.title: King of First rulers of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Lugal-kitun (Sumerian: 𒈗𒆠𒂅, lugal-ki-tun₃; (died c. 2510 BC) was the 12th and last lugal of the first Dynasty of Uruk. He ruled in Mesopotamia in what is now Iraq.

figures.name: Mesh-Ane-pada
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Mesannepada (Sumerian: 𒈩𒀭𒉌𒅆𒊒𒁕, Mesannipàdda [MES-AN-NE2-PAD3-DA]), Mesh-Ane-pada or Mes-Anne-pada ("Youngling chosen by An"; died c. 2525 BC) was the first king listed for the First Dynasty of Ur on the Sumerian king list. He is listed to have ruled for 80 years, having overthrown Lugal-kitun of Uruk: "Then Unug (Uruk) was defeated and the kingship was taken to Urim (Ur)".

figures.name: Meskiagnun
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Meskiagnun, also Mesh-ki-ang-Nanna (Sumerian: 𒈩𒆠𒉘𒉣, Meskiag̃nun [mes-ki-aŋ₂-nun], also 𒀭𒈩𒆠𒉘𒉣𒈾, Meskiag̃nunna [Dmes-ki-aŋ₂-nun-na]; died c. 2450 BC), was the fourth lugal or king of the First Dynasty of Ur, according to the Sumerian King List, which states he ruled for 36 years.

figures.name: Elulu
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Elulu (Sumerian: 𒂊𒇻𒇻, e-lu-lu; fl. c. 2445 BC) is listed as the third king of the First Dynasty of Ur on the Sumerian king list, which states he reigned for 25 years.

figures.name: Balulu
figures.title: King of First dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Balulu (Sumerian: 𒁀𒇻𒇻, ba-lu-lu; fl. c. 2440 BC) was the final king of the First Dynasty of Ur, according to the Sumerian King List, which states he ruled for 36 years:

figures.name: Three
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Awan
figures.figureDescription: 3 (three) is a number, numeral and digit. It is the natural number following 2 and preceding 4, and is the smallest odd prime number and the only prime preceding a square number. (Listed reign: 356 years.)

figures.name: Susuda
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Susada appears as the first king of the second dynasty of Kish in some versions of the Sumerian King List. According to that literary composition, Susada ruled for 201 years. The kings on the early part of the SKL are usually not considered historical, except when they are mentioned in contemporary documents. (Listed reign: 201 years.)

figures.name: Dadasig
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Dadasig appears as the second king of the second dynasty of Kish in some versions of the Sumerian King List. According to that literary composition, Dadasig ruled for 81 years. The kings on the early part of the SKL are usually not considered historical, except when they are mentioned in contemporary documents.

figures.name: Mamagal
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Second dynasty of Kish. Reigned 360 years (mythological length). Epithet: ''"the boatman"''. (Listed reign: 360 years.)

figures.name: Kalbum
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Second dynasty of Kish. Reigned 195 years. Epithet: ''"the son of Mamagal"''.

figures.name: Tuge
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Second dynasty of Kish. Reigned 360 years (mythological length). (Listed reign: 360 years.)

figures.name: Men-nuna
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Second dynasty of Kish. Reigned 180 years. Epithet: ''"the son of Tuge"''.

figures.name: Lugalngu
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Second dynasty of Kish. Reigned 360 years (mythological length). (Listed reign: 360 years.)

figures.name: Hadanish
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Hamazi
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Hamazi. Reigned 360 years (mythological length). (Listed reign: 360 years.)

figures.name: En-shag-kush-ana
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Enshakushanna (Sumerian: 𒂗𒊮𒊨𒀭𒈾, en-sha3-kush2-an-na; fl. c. 2350 BC), or Enshagsagana, En-shag-kush-ana, Enukduanna, En-Shakansha-Ana, En-šakušuana was a king of Uruk around the mid-3rd millennium BC who is named on the Sumerian King List, which states his reign to have been 60 years.

figures.name: Lugal-kinishe-dudu
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Lugal-kinishe-dudu (𒈗𒆠𒉌𒂠𒌌𒌌, lugal-ki-ni-še₃-du₇-du₇) also Lugal-kiginne-dudu  (𒈗𒆠𒁺𒉌𒌌𒌌, lugal-ki-gin-ne2-du₇-du₇; fl. c. 2400 BC), was a King and (ensi) of Uruk and Ur who lived towards the end of the 25th century BC.

figures.name: Argandea
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Second dynasty of Uruk. Reigned 7 years.

figures.name: Nanni
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Nanni is an Italian surname and a masculine Italian given name (as a shortened form of Giovanni). Notable people with the name include:

figures.name: Mesh-ki-ang-Nanna
figures.title: King of Second dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Meskiagnun, also Mesh-ki-ang-Nanna (Sumerian: 𒈩𒆠𒉘𒉣, Meskiag̃nun [mes-ki-aŋ₂-nun], also 𒀭𒈩𒆠𒉘𒉣𒈾, Meskiag̃nunna [Dmes-ki-aŋ₂-nun-na]; died c. 2450 BC), was the fourth lugal or king of the First Dynasty of Ur, according to the Sumerian King List, which states he ruled for 36 years.

figures.name: Lugal-Ane-mundu
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Adab
figures.figureDescription: Lugal-Anne-Mundu (Sumerian: 𒈗𒀭𒉌𒈬𒌦𒆕, lugal-an-ne₂-mu-un-du₃, fl. c. 2500 BC) was the most important king of the city-state of Adab in Sumer.

figures.name: Anbu
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Mari
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Mari. Reigned 30 years.

figures.name: Anba
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Mari
figures.figureDescription: Amba or anba (Arabic: عنبة, Hebrew: עמבה) is a tangy condiment made with mango pickle. Created by Iraqi Jewish merchants in Bombay who purportedly shipped mangoes in vinegar back to Baghdad, Amba bears a resemblance to chutneys from South Asia. The spicy, sweet and sour sauce is typically made of pickled green mangoes, vinegar, salt, turmeric, chilies, and fenugreek.

figures.name: Bazi
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Mari
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Mari. Reigned 30 years. Epithet: ''"the leatherworker"''.

figures.name: Zizi
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Mari
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Mari. Reigned 20 years. Epithet: ''"the fuller"''.

figures.name: Limer
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Mari
figures.figureDescription: A limer, or lymer , was a kind of dog, a scenthound, used on a leash in medieval times to find large game before it was hunted down by the pack. It was sometimes known as a lyam hound/dog  or lime-hound, from the Middle English word lyam, meaning 'leash'. The French cognate limier has sometimes been used for the dogs in English as well.

figures.name: Sharrum-iter
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Mari
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Mari. Reigned 9 years. c. 2350–2341 BC

figures.name: Kug-Bau
figures.title: King of Third dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Kubaba (Sumerian: 𒆬𒀭𒁀𒌑, kug-Dba-u₂) was a legendary Mesopotamian queen who according to the Sumerian King List ruled over Kish for a hundred years before the rise of the dynasty of Akshak. It has been suggested that she was not a historical figure due to anomalies such as the atypical form of the name.

figures.name: Unzi
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akshak
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Akshak. Reigned 30 years.

figures.name: Undalulu
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akshak
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Akshak. Reigned 6 years.

figures.name: Urur
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akshak
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Akshak. Reigned 6 years.

figures.name: Puzur-Nirah
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akshak
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Akshak. Reigned 20 years. c. 2350–2330 BC

figures.name: Ishu-Il
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akshak
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Akshak. Reigned 24 years.

figures.name: Shu-Suen (Akshak)
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akshak
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Dynasty of Akshak. Reigned 7 years. Epithet: ''"the son of Ishu-Il"''.

figures.name: Puzur-Suen (Kish)
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Puzur-Suen (fl. c. 2360 BC) was a king of Sumer, possibly a son of Queen Kugbau, the 1st ruler of the 4th dynasty of Kish.

figures.name: Ur-Zababa
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ur-Zababa (fl. c. 2340 BC) is listed on the Sumerian King List as the second king of the 4th Dynasty of Kish.

figures.name: Zimudar
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Fourth dynasty of Kish. Reigned 30 years.

figures.name: Usi-watar
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Fourth dynasty of Kish. Reigned 7 years. Epithet: ''"the son of Zimudar"''.

figures.name: Eshtar-muti
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Fourth dynasty of Kish. Reigned 11 years.

figures.name: Ishme-Shamash
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Fourth dynasty of Kish. Reigned 11 years.

figures.name: Nanniya
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Fourth dynasty of Kish. Reigned 7 years. c. 2280–2273 BC. Epithet: ''"the jeweller"''.

figures.name: Lugal-zage-si
figures.title: King of Third dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Lugal-Zage-Si (LUGAL.ZAG.GE.SI 𒈗𒍠𒄀𒋛; frequently spelled Lugalzaggesi, sometimes Lugalzagesi or "Lugal-Zaggisi") of Umma (died c. 2334 BC) was the last Sumerian king before the conquest of Sumer by Sargon of Akkad and the rise of the Akkadian Empire, and was considered as the only king of the third dynasty of Uruk, according to the Sumerian King List. Initially, as king of Umma, he led the final victory of Umma in the generation-long conflict with the city-state Lagash for the fertile plain of Gu-Edin.

figures.name: Sargon of Akkad
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akkad
figures.figureDescription: Sargon of Akkad (; Akkadian: 𒊬𒊒𒄀, romanized: Šarrugi; died c. 2279 BC), also known as Sargon the Great, was the first ruler of the Akkadian Empire, known for his conquests of the Sumerian city-states in the 24th to 23rd centuries BC. He is sometimes identified as the first person in recorded history to rule over an empire.

figures.name: Rimush
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akkad
figures.figureDescription: Rimush (or Rimuš, 𒌷𒈬𒍑 Ri-mu-uš; died c. 2270 BC) was the second king of the Akkadian Empire. He was the son of Sargon of Akkad.

figures.name: Manishtushu
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akkad
figures.figureDescription: Manishtushu (Man-ištušu) (𒈠𒀭𒅖𒌅𒋢, Ma-an-ish-tu-su; died c. 2255 BC) was the third king of the Akkadian Empire, reigning 15 years c. 2270 BC until his death c.

figures.name: Naram-Sin of Akkad
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akkad
figures.figureDescription: Naram-Sin, also transcribed Narām-Sîn or Naram-Suen (Akkadian: 𒀭𒈾𒊏𒄠𒀭𒂗𒍪: DNa-ra-am DSîn, meaning "Beloved of the Moon God Sîn", the "𒀭" a determinative marking the name of a god; died c. 2218 BC), was a ruler of the Akkad, who reigned c. 2255–2218 BC (middle chronology), and was the third successor and grandson of King Sargon of Akkad.

figures.name: Shar-Kali-Sharri
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akkad
figures.figureDescription: Shar-Kali-Sharri (𒀭𒊬𒂵𒉌 𒈗𒌷, DShar-ka-li-Sharri; died c. 2193 BC) reigned c. 2218–2193 BC (middle chronology) as the ruler of Akkad.

figures.name: Dudu of Akkad
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akkad
figures.figureDescription: Dudu (Sumerian: 𒁺𒁺, du-du; died c. 2168 BC) was a 22nd-century BC king of Akkad, who reigned for 21 years, c. 2189–2168 BC, according to the Sumerian king list.

figures.name: Shu-Durul
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Akkad
figures.figureDescription: Shu-turul (Shu-durul, 𒋗𒄙𒄒, shu-tur2-ul3 also Šu-Turul; died c. 2154 BC) was the last king of Akkad, ruling for 15 years according to the Sumerian king list. It indicates that he succeeded his father Dudu.

figures.name: Ur-nigin
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Ur-nigin, also Ur-nigina (𒌨𒆸, ur-niŋin) or Ur-nigar (𒌨𒉌𒃻, ur-ni-gar) was a Governor (ensi) of Uruk who lived in 22nd century BC.

figures.name: Ur-gigir
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Ur-gigir (𒌨𒄑𒇀, ur-{gesh}gigir) was the son of Ur-nigin and a Governor (ensi) of Uruk who lived in 22nd century BC.

figures.name: Kuda
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Fourth dynasty of Uruk. Reigned 6 years.

figures.name: Puzur-ili
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Fourth dynasty of Uruk. Reigned 5 years.

figures.name: Ur-Utu
figures.title: King of Fourth dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Fourth dynasty of Uruk. Reigned 25 years. c. 2160–2135 BC. Epithet: ''"the son of Ur-gigir"''.

figures.name: Inkishush
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Inkishush or Inkišuš (fl. late 3rd millennium BC) was the first Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty mentioned on the Sumerian King List. According to this list, he was the successor of Imta. (Listed reign: 6 years.) c. 2200–2194 BC

figures.name: Sarlagab
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Sarlagab or Zarlagab (c. 2200 BC)) was the second Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the Sumerian King List as possibly reigning for six years. (Listed reign: 6 years.)

figures.name: Shulme
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Shulme (fl. late 3rd millennium BC) was the third Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the Sumerian King List. According to the list, he was the successor of Sarlagab. (Listed reign: 6 years.)

figures.name: Elulmesh
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Elulmesh (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the fourth Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the Sumerian King List. While there is virtually no surviving evidence dating from this short timespan (thought to correspond with the first Gutian inroads into Akkadian territory), it has been suggested that this Elulmesh is to be identified as the same as the Akkadian king Ilulu, also known from the King List. (Listed reign: 6 years.)

figures.name: Inimabakesh
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Inimabakesh (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the fifth Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the Sumerian King List. Inimabakesh was the successor of Elulmesh. (Listed reign: 5 years.)

figures.name: Igeshaush
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Igeshaush (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 6th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). Igeshaush was the successor of Inimabakesh. (Listed reign: 6 years.)

figures.name: Yarlagab
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Yarlagab (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 7th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). According to the SKL: Yarlagab was the successor of Igeshaush. (Listed reign: 15 years.)

figures.name: Ibate
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Ibate (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 8th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the Sumerian King List (SKL). (Listed reign: 3 years.)

figures.name: Yarla
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Yarla or Yarlangab (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 9th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). Yarla was the successor of Ibate. (Listed reign: 3 years.)

figures.name: Kurum
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Kurum (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 10th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer, mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). According to the SKL; Kurum was the successor of Yarla. (Listed reign: 1 years.)

figures.name: Apilkin
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Apilkin (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 11th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the Sumerian King List (SKL). According to the SKL, Apilkin was the successor of Kurum and was succeeded by La-erabum. (Listed reign: 3 years.)

figures.name: La-erabum
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: La-erabum or Lasirab (𒆷𒂍𒊏𒀊 la-é-ra-ab also read la-a3-ra-ab, formerly read la-si-ra-ab, fl. circa 2150 BCE) was the 12th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer. (Listed reign: 2 years.)

figures.name: Irarum
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Irarum (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 13th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). According to the SKL: Irarum was the successor of La-erabum. (Listed reign: 2 years.)

figures.name: Ibranum
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Ibranum (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 14th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). According to the SKL: Ibranum was the successor of Irarum. (Listed reign: 1 years.)

figures.name: Hablum
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Hablum (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 15th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). According to the SKL: Hablum was the successor of Ibranum. (Listed reign: 2 years.)

figures.name: Puzur-Suen
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Puzur-Suen (fl. c. 2360 BC) was a king of Sumer, possibly a son of Queen Kugbau, the 1st ruler of the 4th dynasty of Kish. (Listed reign: 7 years.)

figures.name: Yarlaganda
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Yarlaganda (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE) was the 17th Gutian ruler of the Gutian Dynasty of Sumer mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). According to the SKL: Yarlaganda was the successor of Puzur-Suen. (Listed reign: 7 years.)

figures.name: Unknown
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Ruler from the Gutian rule. Reigned 7 years. Si'um or Si-u

figures.name: Tirigan
figures.title: King of Gutian rule
figures.figureDescription: Tirigan (fl. late 3rd millennium BCE, 𒋾𒌷𒂵𒀀𒀭, ti-ri₂-ga-a-an) was the 19th and last Gutian ruler in Sumer mentioned on the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). According to the SKL: Tirigan was the successor of Si'um. (Listed reign: 40 years.)

figures.name: Utu-hengal
figures.title: King of Fifth dynasty of Uruk
figures.figureDescription: Utu-hengal (Sumerian: 𒀭𒌓𒃶𒅅, Dutu-ḫe₂-g̃al₂; died c. 2112 BC), also written Utu-heg̃al, Utu-heĝal, and sometimes transcribed as Utu-hegal, Utu-hejal, Utu-Khengal, was one of the first native kings of Sumer after two hundred years of Akkadian and Gutian rule, and was at the origin of the foundation of the Third Dynasty of Ur by his governor of Ur, Ur-Nammu. He was officially "King of Uruk" in his inscriptions, and is therefore considered as the founder, and only member, of the "Fifth Dynasty of Uruk" (Uruk V).

figures.name: Ur-Namma
figures.title: King of Third dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Ur-Nammu (or Ur-Namma, Ur-Engur, Ur-Gur, Sumerian: 𒌨𒀭𒇉; died c. 2094 BC) was a Sumerian king who founded the Sumerian Third Dynasty of Ur, in southern Mesopotamia, following several centuries of Akkadian and Gutian rule. Though he built many temples and canals his main achievement was building the core of the Ur III Empire through military conquest.

figures.name: Shulgi
figures.title: King of Third dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Shulgi (𒀭𒂄𒄀 dšul-gi, (died c. 2046 BC) formerly read as Dungi) of Ur was the second king of the Third Dynasty of Ur. He reigned for 48 years, from c.

figures.name: Amar-Suena
figures.title: King of Third dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Amar-Sin (Akkadian: 𒀭𒀫𒀭𒂗𒍪: DAmarDSîn, "calf of Sîn", the "𒀭" being a silent honorific for "Divine"; died c. 2037 BC) initially misread as Bur-Sin (c. 2046–2037 BC middle chronology), was the third ruler of the Third Dynasty of Ur.

figures.name: Shu-Suen
figures.title: King of Third dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Shu-Sin, also Šu-Suen (Akkadian: 𒀭𒋗𒀭𒂗𒍪: DŠuDSîn, after the Moon God Sîn", the "𒀭" being a silent honorific for "Divine", formerly read Gimil-Sin; died c. 2028 BC) was king of Sumer and Akkad, and was the fourth king of the Ur III dynasty. He succeeded Amar-Sin, who might have been his father, and reigned c.

figures.name: Ibbi-Suen
figures.title: King of Third dynasty of Ur
figures.figureDescription: Ibbi-Sin (Sumerian: 𒀭𒄿𒉈𒀭𒂗𒍪, Di-bi₂-Dsuen; died c. 2004 BC) was king of Sumer and Akkad and last king of the Ur III dynasty, and reigned c. 2028–2004 BC (Middle chronology).

figures.name: Ishbi-Erra
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Ishbi-Erra (Akkadian: 𒀭𒅖𒁉𒀴𒊏	 diš-bi-ir₃-ra; died c. 1985 BC) was the founder of the dynasty of Isin, reigning from c. 2018 — c.

figures.name: Shu-Ilishu
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Shu-Ilishu (Akkadian: Šu-ilišu; died c. 1975 BC) was the 2nd ruler of the dynasty of Isin.

figures.name: Iddin-Dagan
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Iddin-Dagan (Akkadian: 𒀭𒄿𒁷𒀭𒁕𒃶, Di-din-Dda-gan;  died c. 1954 BC) was the 3rd king of the dynasty of Isin. He is best known for his participation in the sacred marriage rite and the sexually-explicit hymn that described it.

figures.name: Ishme-Dagan
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Ishme-Dagan (Akkadian: 𒀭𒅖𒈨𒀭𒁕𒃶, Diš-me-Dda-gan, Išme-Dagān; died c. 1935 BC) was the 4th king of the First Dynasty of Isin, according to the "Sumerian King List" (SKL). Also according to the SKL: he was both the son and successor of Iddin-Dagan.

figures.name: Lipit-Eshtar
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Lipit-Ishtar (Akkadian: 𒇷𒁉𒀉𒁹𒁯, Lipit-Ištar; died c. 1924 BC) was the 5th king of the First Dynasty of Isin, according to the Sumerian King List. The King List notes that he was the son of Ishme-Dagan, and was succeeded by Ur-Ninurta.

figures.name: Ur-Ninurta
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Ur-Ninurta (died c. 1896 BC) was the 6th king of the 1st Dynasty of Isin. A usurper, Ur-Ninurta seized the throne on the fall of Lipit-Ishtar and held it until his violent death some 28 years later.

figures.name: Bur-Suen
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Būr-Sîn (inscribed  𒀭𒁓𒀭𒂗𒍪 dbur-dEN.ZU; died c. 1874 BC), was the 7th king of the 1st Dynasty of Isin and ruled for 21 years according to the Sumerian King List, 22 years according to the Ur-Isin king list. His reign was characterized by an ebb and flow in hegemony over the religious centers of Nippur and Ur.

figures.name: Lipit-Enlil
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Lipit-Enlil, written dli-pí-it den.líl, where the Sumerian King List and the Ur-Isin king list match on his name and reign  (died c. 1868 BC), was the 8th king of the 1st dynasty of Isin and ruled for around five years, c. 1874–1868 BC (MC).

figures.name: Erra-imitti
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Erra-Imittī, (cuneiform: dèr-ra-i-mit-ti or èr-ra-ZAG.LU meaning “Support of Erra”; died c. 1861 BC) was king of Isin, modern Ishan al-Bahriyat, and according to the Sumerian King List ruled for eight years. He succeeded Lipit-Enlil, with whom his relationship is uncertain and was a contemporary and rival of Sumuel and Nur-Adad of the dynasty of Larsa.

figures.name: Enlil-bani
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Enlil-bani (𒀭𒂗𒆤𒁀𒉌; died c. 1836 BC) was the 10th king of the 1st Dynasty of Isin and reigned 24 years according to the Ur-Isin kinglist. He is best known for the legendary and perhaps apocryphal manner of his ascendancy.

figures.name: Zambiya
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Zambiya, dza-am-bi-ia, (died c. 1833 BC), was the 11th king of the 1st Dynasty of Isin. He is best known for his defeat at the hands of Sin-Iqisham, king of Larsa.

figures.name: Iter-pisha
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Iter-pisha, inscribed in cuneiform as i-te-er-pi/pi4-ša and meaning "Her command is surpassing", (died c. 1829 BC) was the 12th king of Isin during the Old Babylonian period. The Sumerian King List tells us that "the divine Iter-pisha ruled for 4 years." The Ur-Isin King List which was written in the 4th year of the reign of Damiq-ilishu gives a reign of just 3 years.

figures.name: Ur-du-kuga
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Ur-du-kuga, written dur-du6-kù-ga (died c. 1825 BC) was the 13th king of the Dynasty of Isin and reigned for 4 years according to the Sumerian King List, or 3 years according to the Ur-Isin kinglist. He was the third in a sequence of short reigning monarchs whose filiation was unknown and whose power extended over a small region encompassing little more than the city of Isin and its neighbor Nippur.

figures.name: Suen-magir
figures.title: King of Dynasty of Isin
figures.figureDescription: Sîn-māgir (Akkadian: 𒀭𒂗𒍪𒈠𒄫, Dsuen-ma-gir, inscribed dEN.ZU-ma-gir, “Sîn upholds,”; died c. 1814 BC) was the 14th king of Isin and reigned for around 11 years.

figures.name: Nammu
figures.title: Primordial Sea, Mother of Enki
figures.figureDescription: Primordial goddess of the primeval sea who gave birth to Enki. One of the oldest attested Sumerian deities.

figures.name: Samyaza
figures.title: Leader of the 200 Watchers
figures.figureDescription: Chief of the Watchers who organized the oath on Mount Hermon. Taught enchantments and root-cuttings (sorcery). Bound under the earth until judgment; his sons the Nephilim destroyed each other.

figures.name: Azazel
figures.title: Second-in-Command of the Watchers
figures.figureDescription: Bears primary guilt for earth's corruption. Taught metalworking (swords, knives, shields, breastplates), cosmetics (eye-paint, jewelry, bracelets, ornaments, precious stones), and all coloring tinctures. Bound hand and foot in Dudael, covered with sharp rocks.

figures.name: Urakiba
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Arteqoph and Arstikapha.

figures.name: Rameel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Remashel.

figures.name: Kokabiel
figures.title: Chief of the Constellations
figures.figureDescription: Taught portents of the stars and constellations (astronomy/astrology). Commands 365,000 surrogate spirits. Also known as Kakabel, Kochbiel.

figures.name: Tamiel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught the signs of the stars. Also known as Tummiel.

figures.name: Ramiel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught the signs of lightning. Also known as Rumyel. Appears in both fallen and holy angel lists across Enochic traditions.

figures.name: Danel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught the signs of the sun. Also known as Daniel. His name means 'God has judged' or 'God strengthens'.

figures.name: Ezeqeel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught the knowledge of clouds and cloud-reading for divination. Also known as Ziqel.

figures.name: Baraqel
figures.title: Chief of the Astrologers
figures.figureDescription: Taught the signs of lightning and astrology — fate-reading from the stars. Also known as Baraqijal, Barakel. Name means 'Lightning of God'.

figures.name: Armaros
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught the resolving of enchantments and the loosing of spells — counter-magic. Also known as Armers, Armumahel.

figures.name: Batarel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Batraal, Bataryal.

figures.name: Ananel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers.

figures.name: Zaqiel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Zavebe.

figures.name: Samsapeel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Samsaveel, Simapiseel.

figures.name: Satarel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Yetarel.

figures.name: Turiel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Turel, Turyal.

figures.name: Jomjael
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Yomyael, Yomiel, Tumael.

figures.name: Sariel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught the course of the moon — lunar calendrics and reading of lunar phases for omen purposes. Also known as Suriel, Sahriel, Saraquel.

figures.name: Shamsiel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught the signs of the sun — solar omens and solar calendrics. Once a guardian of Eden; serves as an aide to Archangel Uriel. Also known as Samshiel.

figures.name: Penemue
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught mankind the art of writing with ink and paper, and the secrets of wisdom — the bitter and the sweet. His teaching transmitted literacy itself. (1 Enoch 69:8)

figures.name: Gadreel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught humanity all the blows of death — the full apparatus of warfare, expanding on Azazel's metallurgical teaching. (1 Enoch 69:6-7)

figures.name: Araqiel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: Taught the signs of the earth — geomancy, the reading of terrestrial omens. Also known as Arakiel, Arkas, Sarquael.

figures.name: Yeqon
figures.title: The First Tempter
figures.figureDescription: The Watcher who first tempted the other angels into having relations with human women. His accomplices were Asbeel, Gadreel, Penemue, and Kasyade. Also known as Jeqon.

figures.name: Asbeel
figures.title: Accomplice of Yeqon
figures.figureDescription: Accomplice of Yeqon in tempting the Watchers to corrupt themselves with human women. (1 Enoch 69)

figures.name: Kasyade
figures.title: Chief of Spirits
figures.figureDescription: Taught humanity every wicked stroke of spirits and demons, including the stroke of the embryo in the womb. Also known as Kasdaye, Kasadya. (1 Enoch 69)

figures.name: Hermani
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Hermoni.

figures.name: Yehadiel
figures.title: Chief of Tens
figures.figureDescription: One of the twenty chiefs of tens among the Watchers. Also known as Jehaddiel.

figures.name: Enoch
figures.title: Seventh from Adam, the Righteous Scribe
figures.figureDescription: The seventh antediluvian patriarch who walked with God and was translated to heaven without death. Served as scribe of judgment, interceded for the fallen Watchers, and was shown cosmic secrets during his heavenly journeys. His lifespan of 365 years parallels the solar year, mirroring the sun god Shamash and the Mesopotamian king Enmeduranki.

figures.name: Noah
figures.title: The Flood Survivor
figures.figureDescription: The tenth and final antediluvian patriarch. Warned by God of the coming deluge, he built an ark and survived the Great Flood with his family, preserving human and animal life. After the Flood, God established a covenant with him. Parallels the Mesopotamian Ziusudra/Utnapishtim.

figures.name: Michael
figures.title: Chief of the Archangels
figures.domain: Judgment, Binding of the Watchers, Chaos
figures.figureDescription: One of the seven holy archangels. Set over the best part of mankind and over chaos. Tasked with binding Samyaza and the fallen Watchers under the hills of the earth until the day of judgment. Revealed the secret oath to the holy angels.

figures.name: Gabriel
figures.title: Archangel over Paradise
figures.figureDescription: One of the seven holy archangels. Set over Paradise, the serpents, and the Cherubim. Tasked with destroying the children of the Watchers (the Nephilim) by setting them against each other in battle.

figures.name: Uriel
figures.title: Archangel over the World and Tartarus
figures.figureDescription: One of the seven holy archangels. Set over the world and over Tartarus. Sent by God to warn Noah of the coming Flood. Revealed astronomical secrets to Enoch, including the movements of the sun, moon, and stars.

figures.name: Raphael
figures.title: Archangel over the Spirits of Men
figures.domain: Healing, Spirits of Men, Binding of Azazel
figures.figureDescription: One of the seven holy archangels. Set over the spirits of men. Tasked by God with binding Azazel hand and foot, casting him into the darkness of Dudael, and covering him with sharp rocks until the day of judgment.

figures.name: Raguel
figures.title: Archangel of Vengeance
figures.figureDescription: One of the seven holy archangels. Takes vengeance on the world of the luminaries. In Enoch's vision, Raguel explained that the perpetually burning fire was prepared for the persecution of the luminaries of heaven who transgressed the Lord's command.

figures.name: Saraqael
figures.title: Archangel over Sinful Spirits
figures.figureDescription: One of the seven holy archangels. Set over the spirits who sin in the spirit. Oversees the punishment of fallen angels and errant spirits.

figures.name: Remiel
figures.title: Archangel over Those Who Rise
figures.figureDescription: One of the seven holy archangels. Set over those who rise (the resurrection). Presides over the faithful who are raised to eternal life.

figures.name: Haia
figures.title: God of Stores, Father of Ninlil
figures.figureDescription: God of stores and husband of Nisaba. Father of Ninlil (also known as Sud). Sometimes called Haya.

figures.name: Nisaba
figures.title: Goddess of Writing and Grain
figures.figureDescription: Goddess of writing, grain, and surveying. Mother of Ninlil (also called Sud). Also known as Nunbarshegunu.

figures.name: Ningikuga
figures.title: Lady of the Pure Reed
figures.figureDescription: Goddess of reeds and marshes, a consort of Enki. Mother of Ningal.

figures.name: Duttur
figures.title: Ewe Goddess, Mother of Dumuzi
figures.figureDescription: Ewe goddess, mother of Dumuzi and Geshtinanna. Also known as Sirtur.

figures.name: Geshtinanna
figures.title: Goddess of Agriculture and Dream Interpretation
figures.figureDescription: Sister of Dumuzi, goddess of agriculture and dream interpretation. Daughter of Enki and Duttur.

figures.name: Eannatum
figures.title: King of Lagash
figures.figureDescription: Eannatum (Sumerian: 𒂍𒀭𒈾𒁺) was a Sumerian the ensi (ruler) of Lagash c. 2450 BC. He is best known for his victory over the rival city-state of Umma, commemorated on the Stele of the Vultures, one of the earliest known war monuments. Under his reign, Lagash controlled much of Sumer including Ur, Uruk, Larsa, and Kish. He also campaigned against Elam and the mountain peoples of the Zagros.
figures.source: Stele of the Vultures; Lagash inscriptions

figures.name: Entemena
figures.title: King of Lagash
figures.figureDescription: Entemena (Sumerian: 𒂗𒋼𒈨𒈾), son of Eannatum, was a Sumerian king of Lagash who reigned c. 2440–2425 BC. He is known for negotiating a border treaty with Umma after years of conflict over the fertile Gu-Edin plain. His inscriptions describe the construction of canals and temples, including the restoration of the temple of Ningirsu at Girsu.

figures.name: Urukagina
figures.title: King of Lagash
figures.figureDescription: Urukagina (Sumerian: 𒌷𒅗𒄀𒈾; also Uruinimgina) was a Sumerian king of Lagash who reigned c. 2380–2360 BC. He is famous for enacting one of the earliest known legal reforms, recorded on the 'Reform Cylinders' — measures to curb corruption, protect widows and orphans, and reduce the power of the temple bureaucracy. His reign ended when Lugal-zage-si of Umma conquered and destroyed Lagash.
figures.source: Urukagina Reform Cylinders; Sumerian King List

figures.name: Ukush
figures.title: King of Umma
figures.figureDescription: Ukush (also Ush) was a Sumerian king of Umma during the Early Dynastic III period, c. 2370 BC. He is mentioned in the Stele of the Vultures as the adversary of Eannatum of Lagash. He was the father of Lugal-zage-si, who would later unite Sumer under the Third Dynasty of Uruk.
figures.source: Stele of the Vultures; Lagash inscriptions

figures.name: Mesilim
figures.title: King of Kish
figures.figureDescription: Mesilim (also Mesalim) was a Sumerian king of Kish who reigned c. 2600 BC, during the Early Dynastic IIIa period. He is known from inscriptions as the earliest recorded arbitrator in history, having settled the border dispute between the city-states of Lagash and Umma under the authority of the god Enlil. His inscribed mace-heads have been found at Lagash.

figures.name: Anunnaki
figures.title: The Great Gods of Heaven and Earth
figures.figureDescription: A collective of the great gods of Mesopotamian religion, the primary divine council. Their name is often explained as 'those who came down from heaven to earth'. In the oldest Sumerian tradition they were the chthonic deities of the underworld, numbering fifty; in the canonical lists of Akkadian religion they are usually the seven great gods (Anu, Enlil, Enki, Ninhursag, Nanna, Utu, Inanna). In Atrahasis the Anunnaki are the seven great gods who sit in council and decide the fate of the Igigi.

figures.name: Igigi
figures.title: The Gods of Heaven / The Divine Workforce
figures.figureDescription: A collective of the gods who in Atrahasis serve as the heavenly workforce, digging the rivers Tigris and Euphrates under the oversight of the Anunnaki. When their labor becomes unbearable they rebel and march on the dwelling of Enlil, prompting the creation of mankind from the clay and the blood of the slain god to take over their work. Sometimes identified with the great gods of heaven, sometimes distinguished from them; the precise rank of the Igigi relative to the Anunnaki varies by tradition.

places.name: Eridu
places.placeDescription: First city ever built according to Sumerian tradition. Sacred city of Enki.

places.name: Uruk
places.placeDescription: Great walled city ruled by Gilgamesh. Center of Inanna worship.

places.name: Ur
places.placeDescription: City of the moon god Nanna. Site of the great ziggurat.

places.name: Nippur
places.placeDescription: Holy city of Enlil. Religious center of Sumer where the gods held council.

places.name: Babylon
places.placeDescription: City of Marduk. Became the supreme city when Marduk rose to kingship of the gods.

places.name: Kish
places.placeDescription: First city to receive kingship after the Flood. Etana ruled here.

places.name: E-kur
places.placeDescription: Temple of Enlil in Nippur. 'Mountain House' — the most important temple in Sumer.

places.name: E-abzu
places.placeDescription: Temple of Enki in Eridu. Built over the slain Apsu.

places.name: Kur
places.placeDescription: The underworld / land of the dead. Ruled by Ereshkigal. Inanna descended here.

places.name: An
places.placeDescription: The heavens. Realm of Anu. Where the gods held their celestial court.

places.name: Cedar Forest
places.placeDescription: Sacred forest guarded by Humbaba. Gilgamesh and Enkidu journeyed here.

places.name: Mount Mashu
places.placeDescription: Twin-peaked mountain where the sun rises and sets. Gilgamesh passed through on his quest.

places.name: Adab
places.placeDescription: Capitol city of the Adab region in ancient Mesopotamia.

places.name: Akkad
places.placeDescription: Capitol city of the Akkad region in ancient Mesopotamia.

places.name: Akshak
places.placeDescription: Capitol city of the Akshak region in ancient Mesopotamia.

places.name: Awan
places.placeDescription: Capitol city of the Awan region in ancient Mesopotamia.

places.name: Hamazi
places.placeDescription: Capitol city of the Hamazi region in ancient Mesopotamia.

places.name: Isin
places.placeDescription: Capitol city of the Isin region in ancient Mesopotamia.

places.name: Mari
places.placeDescription: Capitol city of the Mari region in ancient Mesopotamia.

places.name: Mount Hermon
places.modernLocation: Anti-Lebanon mountain range, on the border between Syria and Lebanon
places.placeDescription: The mountain where the 200 Watchers descended and swore an oath under Samyaza's leadership to take human wives. Considered the site of the Watchers' rebellion.

places.name: Dudael
places.modernLocation: Desert wilderness (location uncertain; possibly near the Dead Sea)
places.placeDescription: The desert pit where the archangel Raphael bound Azazel hand and foot, covering him with rugged and sharp rocks. Azazel was imprisoned here until the day of judgment.

places.name: Sheol
places.placeDescription: The underworld realm of the dead, described in Enoch's vision as a place with hollows and compartments where the spirits of the dead await judgment. Includes the place of punishment for the fallen angels, with a great burning fire.

places.name: Paradise
places.placeDescription: The Garden of Righteousness, a heavenly realm where the tree of life stands. In Enoch's vision, it is located among seven magnificent mountains in the north-west. The dwelling place of the righteous after death, reserved for those who have not been corrupted by the Watchers' teachings.

places.name: Lagash
places.placeDescription: Major Sumerian city-state, capital of the Lagash region under the Second dynasty of Lagash. Patron deity Ningirsu/Ninurta. Gudea of Lagash ruled here.

places.name: Larsa
places.placeDescription: Important Sumerian city-state and cult center of the sun god Utu. Capital of the Kingdom of Larsa during the Isin-Larsa period.

places.name: Sippar
places.placeDescription: Ancient Sumerian city on the Euphrates. Major cult center of Utu (Shamash) and the home of the Babylonian sun god. Site of the Ebabbar temple.

places.name: Susa
places.placeDescription: Capital of Elam, one of the oldest cities in the world. Important in SKL as the seat of the Awan dynasty. Major political and economic center.

places.name: Shuruppak
places.placeDescription: Antediluvian Sumerian city. Home of Ziusudra/Utnapishtim, the Sumerian flood hero. Mentioned in the Sumerian King List as the seat of the last king before the Flood.
places.source: Sumerian King List; Epic of Gilgamesh

places.name: Umma
places.placeDescription: Sumerian city-state, rival of Lagash. Patron deity Shara (son of Inanna). Important center for the cult of Shara and the Umma-Lagash border conflict.

places.name: Bad-tibira
places.placeDescription: Antediluvian Sumerian city mentioned in the SKL as the second city to hold kingship before the Flood. Also known as Patibira. Associated with Dumuzi and the metalworking god Enki.

places.name: Borsippa
places.placeDescription: Sumerian city near Babylon. Major cult center of Nabu, the god of wisdom and writing. Site of the Ezida temple and a large ziggurat.

places.name: Kutha
places.placeDescription: Sumerian city north of Nippur. Cult center of Nergal, god of plague and the underworld. Site of the Emeslam temple.

places.name: Dilbat
places.placeDescription: Sumerian city south of Babylon. Cult center of the god Uraš (also known as Urash of Dilbat). Known for its temple of Uraš named the E-ibbi-Anum.

places.name: Girsu
places.modernLocation: Tell Telloh, Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
places.placeDescription: Girsu (Sumerian: 𒄈𒋢𒆠 ĝirsu; modern Tell Telloh) was a city of the Sumerian city-state of Lagash. It was the religious center of Lagash, home to the temple of the patron god Ningirsu. The Stele of the Vultures was discovered here, as were numerous administrative tablets from the Early Dynastic and Ur III periods.

places.name: Gu-Edin
places.placeDescription: Gu-Edin (also Gu'edena, meaning 'Edge of the Plain' in Sumerian) was a fertile agricultural plain located on the border between the Sumerian city-states of Lagash and Umma. This land was the subject of a generations-long border conflict, one of the earliest recorded wars in human history.

places.name: Aratta
places.modernLocation: Possibly eastern Iran or the Armenian Highlands
places.placeDescription: Aratta was a legendary kingdom described in Sumerian literature as a wealthy, mountainous land rich in gold, silver, and lapis lazuli. It was the rival of Uruk during the reigns of the legendary kings Enmerkar and Lugalbanda. Its exact geographical location is unknown, with scholarly theories placing it in eastern Iran, the Caspian region, or Armenia.

places.name: Dabrum
places.placeDescription: Dabrum (also Dubrum) was a city mentioned in the victory stele of Utu-hengal of Uruk. The citizens of Dabrum captured the fleeing Gutian king Tirigan and his family, handing them over to Utu-hengal. Its exact location is unknown.

places.name: E-anna
places.placeDescription: Temple of Inanna in Uruk. 'House of Heaven' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒀭 e₂-anna) was one of the oldest and most important temples in Mesopotamia, dating to the Uruk period (c. 4000 BCE). The White Temple built atop the Anu Ziggurat was part of this vast sacred precinct.

places.name: E-babbar
places.modernLocation: Tell Abu Habbah, Babil Governorate, Iraq
places.placeDescription: Temple of Utu/Shamash in Sippar. 'White House' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒌓𒌓 e₂-babbar) was the main cult center of the sun god in northern Babylonia. A second E-babbar existed in Larsa.

places.name: E-ninnu
places.modernLocation: Tell Telloh, Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
places.placeDescription: Temple of Ningirsu/Ninurta in Girsu. 'House of Fifty' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒉌𒉣𒉣 e₂-ninnu) was the most important temple in the Lagash state. Eannatum and Entemena richly endowed it with votive offerings and inscriptions.

places.name: E-gishnugal
places.modernLocation: Tell Muqayyar, Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
places.placeDescription: Temple of Nanna/Sin in Ur. 'House of Great Light' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒄑𒉣𒃲 e₂-giš-nun-gal) was the great moon temple complex of Ur, part of which was the famous ziggurat built by Ur-Namma (c. 2100 BCE).

places.name: Esagila
places.placeDescription: Temple of Marduk in Babylon. 'House That Lifts Its Head' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒊕𒅍𒆷 e₂-sag-ila₂) was the most important temple in Babylonia during the late period. The annual Akitu (New Year) festival was celebrated here.

places.name: Etemenanki
places.placeDescription: The great ziggurat of Marduk in Babylon. 'House of the Foundation of Heaven and Underworld' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒋼𒀀𒆠 e₂-temen-an-ki) is widely believed to be the inspiration for the biblical Tower of Babel. Built by Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II.

places.name: E-meslam
places.placeDescription: Temple of Nergal in Kutha. 'House of the Meslam' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒈩𒇴 e₂-mes-lam) was the temple of the underworld god Nergal. Meslam also became an epithet of the god himself.

places.name: E-zida
places.placeDescription: Temple of Nabu in Borsippa. 'True House' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒍣𒁕 e₂-zida) was the most important temple of the scribe god Nabu. Its ziggurat, Eurmeiminanki, was a prominent landmark visible from Babylon.

places.name: E-galmah
places.placeDescription: Temple of Gula/Ninisinna in Isin. 'Great House' (Sumerian: 𒂍𒃲𒈤 e₂-galmah) was the primary temple of Gula, the goddess of healing, and the center of a major healing cult in ancient Mesopotamia.

events.name: Slaying of Apsu
events.eventDescription: Enki/Ea put Apsu into a deep sleep and slew him, then built his temple upon the body.

events.name: Slaying of Tiamat
events.eventDescription: Marduk defeated Tiamat in single combat, split her body to form heaven and earth.

events.name: Creation of Mankind
events.eventDescription: Enki and Ninhursag created humans from clay mixed with the blood of the slain god Kingu.

events.name: Inanna's Descent to the Underworld
events.eventDescription: Inanna descended through the seven gates of the underworld to confront her sister Ereshkigal.

events.name: The Great Flood
events.eventDescription: Enlil decreed the destruction of mankind by flood. Enki warned Ziusudra who built an ark and survived.

events.name: Gilgamesh and Enkidu Slay Humbaba
events.eventDescription: Gilgamesh and Enkidu journeyed to the Cedar Forest and slew its guardian Humbaba.

events.name: Death of Enkidu
events.eventDescription: The gods decreed Enkidu's death as punishment for slaying Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven.

events.name: Gilgamesh Seeks Immortality
events.eventDescription: After Enkidu's death, Gilgamesh journeyed to find Utnapishtim and the secret of eternal life.

events.name: Etana's Ascent to Heaven
events.eventDescription: King Etana rode an eagle to heaven seeking the plant of birth to produce an heir.

events.name: Founding of Eridu
events.eventDescription: The first city was established by the gods. Kingship first descended from heaven here.

events.name: The Fall of the Watchers
events.eventDescription: Two hundred Watcher angels under the leadership of Samyaza descended on Mount Hermon, swore an oath to bind themselves together, and took human wives. They fathered the Nephilim, giants who consumed the labor of mankind. The Watchers also taught humanity forbidden knowledge: sorcery, weapon-making, cosmetics, astrology, and divination.

events.name: The Binding of Azazel
events.eventDescription: God commanded Raphael to bind Azazel hand and foot, cast him into the darkness of Dudael, and cover him with rugged and sharp rocks. Azazel was to remain there until the great day of judgment, when he would be cast into the fire.

events.name: The Binding of the Watchers
events.eventDescription: God commanded Michael to bind Samyaza and his associates under the hills of the earth for seventy generations until the day of judgment. The Watchers were to be cast into the abyss of fire for eternity. Their sons, the Nephilim, were destroyed by being set against each other with the sword.

events.name: Enoch's Heavenly Journeys
events.eventDescription: Enoch was taken by the angels and shown the mysteries of heaven and earth. He visited the heavenly temple and saw God's throne of glory, the dwelling places of the righteous, the places of punishment for the wicked, the tree of life, the seven mountains, and the storehouses of the winds and luminaries. The archangel Uriel revealed to him the movements of the sun, moon, and stars.

events.name: The Deluge Judgment
events.eventDescription: God decreed the destruction of all flesh by the Great Flood as judgment for the corruption brought by the Watchers and the Nephilim. Uriel was sent to warn Noah to build an ark. The Flood cleansed the earth, preserving only Noah and his family. The Watchers were already bound and awaiting final judgment.

events.name: Sargon Conquers Sumer
events.eventDescription: Sargon of Akkad defeated Lugal-Zage-Si of Uruk and conquered all of Sumer, unifying the region under Akkadian rule for the first time in history. This marked the beginning of the Akkadian Empire, the first territorial empire in Mesopotamia.
events.source: Sumerian King List; Sargon of Akkad inscriptions

events.name: Founding of Akkad
events.eventDescription: Sargon built the city of Akkad (Agade) as his imperial capital. The city's exact location remains unknown but was likely near the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Akkad became the richest and most powerful city in Mesopotamia during the Akkadian period.

events.name: Great Revolt Against Naram-Sin
events.eventDescription: A massive coalition of Sumerian city-states, led by kings from Kish, Uruk, Ur, and other cities, rebelled against Akkadian rule. Naram-Sin defeated the coalition in nine major battles in a single year, as recorded in the 'Great Revolt' inscriptions. This event marked the beginning of Naram-Sin's deification.

events.name: Fall of Akkad
events.eventDescription: The Akkadian Empire collapsed under pressure from Gutian invasions, internal rebellion, and possibly severe drought. The Gutians overran Mesopotamia, and the city of Akkad was destroyed. The 'Curse of Akkad' literary work describes the devastation as divine punishment for Naram-Sin's sacrilege.
events.source: Sumerian King List; Curse of Akkad

events.name: Ur-Namma Founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
events.eventDescription: Ur-Namma (also known as Ur-Nammu), a governor of Ur under Utu-Hegal of Uruk, rose to power and founded the Third Dynasty of Ur after defeating the Gutians and re-establishing Sumerian independence. He reunified Sumer and ushered in the 'Sumerian Renaissance.'

events.name: Ur-Namma Builds the Great Ziggurat of Ur
events.eventDescription: Ur-Namma constructed the Great Ziggurat of Ur (Etemenniguru), a massive stepped pyramid dedicated to the moon god Nanna/Sin. The ziggurat measured approximately 64 by 46 meters at its base and stood about 30 meters tall. It remains one of the best-preserved ziggurats in Mesopotamia.

events.name: Code of Ur-Nammu
events.eventDescription: Ur-Namma issued the earliest known written law code, predating Hammurabi's code by more than three centuries. The code established justice, protected the weak from the powerful, set fixed prices and wages, and prescribed punishments for various offenses. Only fragments survive on clay tablets.

events.name: Shulgi's Administrative Reforms
events.eventDescription: King Shulgi reformed the entire Ur III state apparatus, standardizing weights and measures, creating a centralized bureaucracy, establishing a system of messenger stations with royal roads, reorganizing the military, and commissioning extensive building projects. He also declared himself a god and promoted the cult of the deified king.
events.source: Shulgi hymns; administrative tablets from Ur III period

events.name: Fall of Ur
events.eventDescription: The city of Ur was sacked by the Elamites and their allies, ending the Third Dynasty of Ur. King Ibbi-Sin was taken captive to Elam. This catastrophic event was mourned in the 'Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur,' one of the most famous Sumerian literary compositions describing the city's complete devastation.
events.source: Sumerian King List; Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur

events.name: Ishbi-Erra Founds the Dynasty of Isin
events.eventDescription: Ishbi-Erra, a former official of Ibbi-Sin of Ur, established himself at Isin and founded a new dynasty after the fall of Ur.
